title: A Judge Pauses the Giant Arch
summary:
A judge paused a giant arch in Washington, D.C., just after it won approval. Just before midnight on Thursday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan blocked building for 14 days at the request of Washington, D.C., and Virginia.

The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Her 33-page opinion said local governments would likely be harmed by traffic problems.

Less than two hours earlier, the National Capital Planning Commission had approved the arch 8 to 4. It heard nearly eight hours of talks, and about 131 people signed up to speak, most against it.

Critics said it would block a view, make busy airspace less safe, and disrespect service members buried nearby. They also asked if it is legal and what it would cost, which is still unknown.

Supporters, including two Republican members of Congress, called it a tribute to the nation and to those who served, saying Congress approved the idea in 1925, when it approved two tall columns for the same place that were never built. Lawsuits from Vietnam War veterans, an architectural historian, and D.C. and Virginia are still in court, so for now the arch is on hold.
why_it_matters: It matters because the arch would change a place many families visit to remember service members, and the pause gives the courts time to decide whether it should be built there.
